Commentary.Commentary: We are back for the chase! The umpires are out in the middle and so are the players of Sri Lanka. It will be the southpaw duo of Saim Ayub and Fakhar Zaman to open the innings for Pakistan. Asitha Fernando will get proceedings underway with the ball. Let's go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Right then, 289 is what Pakistan need to seal the series win and given what we have seen in the last hour or so, the surface has gotten much better for batting. Sri Lanka will be hoping that their pacers come good early in the chase, as the conditions will just keep getting better for the chasing side. This could well turn out to be another humdinger of a contest, so don't go anywhere as the run chase will start in a bit.

Sri Lanka's middle-order batter, Kamindu Mendis is down for a chat. He says that they were targeting 300 runs but eventually they got to 288, which is also a good score. On his role in this team, he says that he is the designated finisher and he has been able to do the job in Tests but hasn't quite replicated the same in ODIs. Feels that the surface did improve for batting later on but also feels that their quicks will enjoy bowling in the first Powerplay.

Pakistan won't be too pleased with the total on the board and they will certainly feel that they let the Lankans off the hook. The frontline pacers were largely ineffective to begin with and Haris Rauf was being hit for plenty of runs. However, a run out and then a stellar spell from Abrar Ahmed saw the hosts take complete control of the match. One expected the other spinners to chime in and take advantage of an abrasive surface but the likes of Mohammad Nawaz and Saim Ayub couldn't get going. Rauf did come back in to pick up wickets at different junctures but again, didn't receive much support from the other pacers. All in all, a hot and cold outing with the ball for Pakistan.

Sri Lanka were asked to bat first on a surface that looked quite different from the last game but the Lankans started very strongly. However, a run out in the 10th over started a shaky period for the visitors and they found themselves 98/4 at one stage. The middle order did step up and the likes of Sadeera Samarawickrama, Janith Liyanage and Kamindu Mendis all contributed but only Liyanage notched up a fifty, but he too couldn't convert it into a big score. Towards the end, it seemed like the visitors were heading to an under-par total but Wanindu Hasaranga made sure that they played the full 50 overs and got to a solid total.

End of what seemed to be a simmering first innings with the bat from Sri Lanka but Wanindu Hasaranga has given them the lift-off they needed. Pakistan did well after the first Powerplay to pick up wickets in a heap but did let a couple of crucial partnerships to build and couldn't finish things tidily with the ball. At the mid-game interval, the visitors will be the happier side and will definitely feel that 288 is a very defendable score on this deck.

Reckons that the surface will still be good for batting but the spinners will have a bigger role to play as well.

The captain of Sri Lanka, Charith Asalanka, says that the surface looks different than the other day but it looks like a decent pitch. Adds that even though they lost the first game, there were a lot of positives but the last 15 overs were an area of concern. Agha stated that they aim to start the game strongly, emphasizing the importance of a good beginning in white-ball cricket. All eyes will be on the Rawalpindi pitch once again, which is expected to remain batting-friendly with an average first-innings score near 287, while still offering significant bounce and seam movement for the fast bowlers. The toss will be a key factor, as the team bowling first has shown a clear advantage in recent ODIs at this venue. For Sri Lanka, the match is a must-win to keep the series alive and force a decider, promising a high-stakes, competitive contest against a Pakistan side determined to wrap up a valuable home series victory. Stay tuned for the all-important toss and team news.

Sri Lanka, on the other hand, will enter the game with a point to prove, having fallen just six runs short in a high-scoring chase in the first ODI. Their batting showed promise with multiple players getting starts, but the crucial missing element was a batter converting their effort into a match-winning century, a feat that eluded even Wanindu Hasaranga's valiant late half-century. Pakistan takes a slender 1-0 lead into the second One Day International in Rawalpindi, knowing that a win here will seal the series against a determined Sri Lankan side. The first match was a high-scoring thriller, decided by a narrow six-run margin, which proved that these two teams are closely matched despite the different routes they took to reach the finish line. Sri Lanka will be desperate to bounce back and level the series, turning the final game into a decider, while Pakistan will be aiming for a more clinical performance to wrap things up swiftly on their home ground. For Pakistan, the win was a massive success story for their middle order, who stepped up when the top order struggled. The century by Salman Ali Agha, paired with Hussain Talat's vital half-century, showed grit and the depth of Pakistan's batting. However, the team will be concerned by the bad starts in both innings. Their pacers struggled with line and length early in the chase, and the top-order batters also failed to build a foundation. Haris Rauf's destructive spell of 4/61 remains the blueprint for their bowling attack, and Pakistan will look for him, along with Naseem Shah and Mohammad Nawaz, to be lethal right from the first ball. Sri Lanka, meanwhile, has plenty of positives despite the defeat. Their opening batters started the chase brilliantly, showing they can handle the pace challenge. Also, their main weapon, Wanindu Hasaranga, was outstanding. Not only did he spin a web around the Pakistan middle-order with his three wickets, but his battling half-century nearly snatched an unlikely victory for his team. The primary concern for the visitors will be their collapses in both departments. They dominated with the ball initially before Agha and Talat took over, and they were cruising with the bat before Rauf triggered a massive slump. They need key batters like Mendis, Sadeera Samarawickrama and Charith Asalanka to convert starts into big scores to reduce the pressure on their lower order. The game was originally scheduled to be played on the 13th of November but due to unfortunate events taking place in Islamabad, it has now been moved to the 14th of November. Given the nature of the Rawalpindi pitch, which typically favors the batters and saw Pakistan post nearly 300 runs in the first game, we can expect another high-scoring affair.
